facts.fact: Fish swim up to the surface because the water there has the most dissolved oxygen.
Gasping at the surface can be an early warning of a wider problem in the tank, so treat it as a reason to investigate.
If the cause is nitrite poisoning or zero oxygen, fish can die within hours.
Merck lists 'piping' at the surface as the behavioural sign of hypoxia (low dissolved oxygen), with flared gills and dark colouring as physical signs.
In hypoxia, large fish are affected more than small fish.
Fish short of oxygen are lethargic, gasp at the surface and gather around water returns.
The signs of hypoxia look like a gill problem, so a dissolved-oxygen test is needed to confirm it.
Nitrite toxicity also causes piping at the surface, and the gills and blood turn dark brown, though this is hard to see.
Carbon dioxide toxicity shows as lethargy at the surface.
Gasping first thing in the morning points to oxygen running out overnight in planted tanks or ponds.
Spots, clamped fins or signs of fungal or bacterial infection alongside gasping point to gill disease rather than water chemistry.
Suspect gill disease if fish keep gasping when oxygen is not low, especially with discoloured gills, extra mucus, rubbing (flashing) or reduced feeding.
In mild oxygen shortage, fish still swim fast and dive when startled by a hand clap. In severe shortage, they bunch up, ignore noise or are still at the surface around 8–9 a.m.
Mild oxygen shortage shows in the early morning. In severe shortage, fish stay at the surface day and night, become sluggish, stop eating and can die in large numbers.

Betta splendens is a facultative air-breather and the blue gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus) is an obligate air-breather. Both use a labyrinth organ, so regular trips to the surface for air are normal for them.
High water temperature reduces how much oxygen the water can hold.
A heater stuck 'on' can overheat the tank, often to well over 30°C (86°F).
Ammonia increases mucus on the gills and makes them less efficient.
Nitrite reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.
Nitrite binds haemoglobin and turns the blood brown (brown-blood disease). The effect is worse when dissolved oxygen is low.
Too much CO2, from over-dosing or a faulty CO2 unit in a planted tank, can cause gasping.
Merck gives a CO2 toxicity threshold of more than 40 mg/L.
Merck gives a nitrite toxicity threshold of NO2 above 0.1 mg/L, made worse by low chloride in fresh water.
Most test kits measure NO2-N. Multiply the reading by 3.3 to get NO2 in mg/L.
Merck links ammonia toxicity to un-ionized ammonia above 1 mg/L and pH above 8, typical of 'new tank syndrome'.
High stocking, heavy feeding and a dirty pond or filter use up oxygen as organic waste breaks down.
Submerged plants respire at night and then use more oxygen than they make.
Low oxygen is most likely in summer and often happens in the early hours of the morning.
Long spells of heavy rain or overcast weather reduce algal photosynthesis, so less oxygen is produced during the day.
Parasites, pathogens or chemicals that damage the gills can cause gasping even when oxygen is not very low.
Ammonia (NH3) becomes more toxic as pH and temperature rise.
Check the water temperature first and cool the tank if it is too warm.
Increase aeration. If fish gasp in the morning, aerate especially at night.
Test the water at the first sign of trouble. If ammonia or nitrite is present, do an immediate water change with dechlorinated tap water.
Practical Fishkeeping recommends a 50% emergency water change.
If a CO2 unit has released too much gas, cut CO2 dosing and increase aeration.
Additional aeration helps a hypoxic system, but you must also find and fix the cause.
Reduce or stop feeding for a short time, then bring feeding back gradually once the fish are stable.
When changing water, check the new water and how much it differs from the tank or pond water, so the fish are not shocked.
In a power outage, a battery-powered air pump with an airstone is the simplest backup.

During an outage, don't feed and turn off automatic feeders for the first 1–2 hours. After 8+ hours, run an air stone or sponge filter for 1 hour every 8 hours, or every 4 hours if the tank is heavily stocked or fish are gasping.
Chloride competes with nitrite at the gills. A chloride level 20 times the nitrite-nitrogen level completely counteracts nitrite toxicity in channel catfish and probably most freshwater species.
Fish with brown-blood disease recover quickly once moved to water with little nitrite.
To limit nitrite toxicity, keep dissolved oxygen above 3 mg/L for warmwater fish or 5 mg/L for coldwater fish.
Replace a heater that is malfunctioning.
For suspected gill disease, consult a specialist dealer or an experienced fish vet.
Don't use chemicals or several products at once on your own. If deaths rise fast or fish show unusual lesions, call an aquaculture technician.
After power returns, test ammonia and nitrite and do water changes if either reads above 0 ppm.
After an outage, rinse the filter and clean the impellers before restarting, because clogged impellers often fail to start.
Keep a tropical freshwater tank at about 24–28°C (75–82°F).
Low dissolved oxygen is indicated below about 5–6 ppm (mg/litre). Cheap DO test kits are available.
When testing DO, follow the kit instructions carefully. Shaking or pouring the sample adds oxygen and skews the result.
Feed only what fish need, manage stocking density and clean regularly to keep organic waste from building up.
Monitor oxygen regularly where possible, especially near dawn and after overcast days.
Keep a battery air pump with spare airstones, airline tubing and batteries for power outages.
Aquarium Co-Op's battery air pump switches on automatically in an outage and runs about 20 hours, or 40+ hours in a 15-seconds-on, 15-seconds-off power-save mode.
Safe long-term nitrite-nitrogen is about 0.5–2.5 mg/L for warmwater fish and freshwater invertebrates, and 0.0125–0.5 mg/L for coldwater fish.
Don't always blame temperature. Sudden gasping is often linked to pollution or disease.
Gasping alone is not enough to know the cause. Combine watching the fish with water tests.
Don't wait until fish crowd the surface before adding oxygen.
Don't stir up bottom mud suddenly, because it can release toxic gases into the water.
Canister filters can go anoxic in as little as 4–6 hours without power. Restarting them uncleaned can flush rotting debris into the tank.
Don't feed for 24 hours after power returns, so the biological filter can catch up.
A Phú Thọ provincial agriculture department page lists hot, muggy summer weather, overfeeding and dawn oxygen shortage as causes of fish surfacing ('cá nổi đầu').
Vietnamese technical pages use the terms 'cá nổi đầu' and 'ngáp khí' for fish gasping at the surface.
A Vietnamese maker of biological products sells Microbe-Lift AQUA SA and AQUA C bacteria to break down organic waste and reduce H2S and NH3. These are pond products.
Nitrite sensitivity varies widely by species. Coldwater fish such as rainbow trout (96-h LC50 0.24–11.0 mg/L NO2-N) are far more sensitive than common carp (88.0 mg/L).
Merck notes that gas supersaturation can cause gas bubbles in the gills, fins and eyes, and fine bubbles may appear on the aquarium glass.
Most fish can go about a week without food, so skipping meals during an outage is safe.
